quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

The tree cites an 1860 census (S2) for the Thomas to Patrick link, but no search of it is logged. 1860 is name-searchable and fills the gap between 1850 (Patrick age 5) and 1870, showing whether the same household, the mother and any siblings persist. Variant spellings Flinn, Flynn, Flin.

The 1880 census is name-searchable and records each person's relationship to the head and the birthplaces of both parents, so it is the best census for parentage. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials is name-searchable. Plan this as the subject's own death item because a baptism may not exist: he was probably born in Ireland ca. 1845, and civil birth registration there and in Pennsylvania did not cover this period.

Burial and obituary trail for Patrick's own death in March 1908: cemetery records (Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, name-searchable) and local newspaper obituary. They can name the burial parish, relatives and a family plot shared with Thomas Flynn or siblings, which is FAN evidence on the parents.

Patrick's own marriage, expected after he reached adulthood around 1865-1880. Church and county marriage records often give age and birthplace, and a church entry may name parents. Also yields his wife and children, whose baptisms name sponsors (FAN) and whose records may name grandparents. Collections Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Marriages are name-searchable.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) to the mother, expected before Patrick's birth around 1845. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (and a maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so also check whether Thomas had an earlier or later wife), and by its date corroborate Thomas as father; it does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Because the tree gives Ireland as the birthplace, the marriage may be in Ireland (Catholic parish registers) rather than Pennsylvania; no Ireland locality survey is in the project, so that search needs a survey first. Search Pennsylvania marriage collections too.

Roman Catholic registers (probably, for Irish immigrants) are held at the parish or diocese, not the county (loc_001), and some anthracite-region films are browse-only. Seek sacramental entries for Patrick, Thomas and the mother (burials, siblings' baptisms, sponsors) and Patrick's own marriage. Use volume_search for browse-only registers; the Diocese of Philadelphia and successors hold these.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could have died anywhere from 1850 to about 1910, so the window is sized to his lifespan, not Patrick's. Register of Wills records (from 1811) can name heirs and children. Pennsylvania Probate Records is name-searchable but thin; Wills and Deeds is also name-searchable; otherwise browse the county images. Include the mother's estate.

Patrick would have been about 16-20 during the Civil War; the Pennsylvania Register of Military Volunteers is name-searchable and may give birthplace and residence, and pension files (NARA) can name family. Also a FAN lead through enlistment companions. Lower priority.

After those come Thomas's will or estate, brothers and sisters and neighbours, Civil War and naturalization papers. The order runs from the records most likely to answer outright to those that only corroborate. He was probably born in Ireland, so a Pennsylvania baptism may not exist, which is why his own death, burial and marriage entries come early.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Here's what the research-plan agent found and built for question q_001 — **Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. c. 1843, Baiersbronn)?**

---

## Where Her Parents Would Be Recorded

Katharina was born in **Baiersbronn, Württemberg**, so her parents would appear in the **Protestant church books of that parish**:
- Baptism register (the primary source — names the parents directly)
- Familienregister (a page-per-family summary with parents, marriage, and children)
- Parents' own marriage record (gives the mother's maiden name)
- Siblings' baptisms and godparents (FAN cluster)
- Katharina's own marriage/death entries (often state parents and birthplace)

**Important:** These records are **not on FamilySearch**. They are only available on **Archion**, a paid German archive site.

---

## Your 6-Step Research Plan (pl_001)

| # | What to Search | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| pli_001 | Katharina's baptism, 1842–1844 | Archion, Baiersbronn | Names parents directly |
| pli_002 | Familienregister, 1800–1900 | Archion, Baiersbronn | Lists parents, marriage, children together |
| pli_003 | Parents' marriage record, 1815–1843 | Archion, Baiersbronn | Gives mother's maiden name |
| pli_004 | Sibling baptisms & godparents, 1830–1860 | Archion, Baiersbronn | FAN cluster corroboration |
| pli_005 | Katharina's marriage & death/burial, 1860–1920 | Archion, Baiersbronn + neighbouring parishes | Fallback if baptism not found; often state parents |
| pli_006 | MyHeritage discovery search, Württemberg, 1830–1920 | MyHeritage | Leads only — check against church originals |

---

## What to Do Next

1. **Open Archion**: Go to the [Baiersbronn page on Archion](https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn). You'll need an Archion account.
2. **Search the baptism book for 1842–1844** for a *Katharina* (also *Catharina* or *Katarina*) *Seeger* (also *Seger* or *Säger*). Note the father's and mother's names, any godparents, and the date.
3. **Then check the Familienregister** to confirm the family unit.

The next step belongs to the **search-external-sites** skill for the Archion and MyHeritage plan items. If you don't have an Archion account, let me know and we can lean more heavily on MyHeritage instead.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

**Mode:** create. No plan existed for q_001: "Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?"

**What the tree already records:**
- Michael (I1) lived in Pennsylvania in 1870. log_001 gives him as a farmer in a county other than Schuylkill.
- Michael lived in Schuylkill County in 1882 as a miner (F2 and F3, log_002 directory).
- His brother Patrick (I2) lived in Schuylkill County in 1875 (F4). Source S2 is a deed, Deed Book 42, p. 118, in which Patrick bought land from James Kelly in 1875.
- Both brothers are children of the same unnamed Sheahan parent entry (I3). Nothing names the parents or says where the family came from.
- No person has an ark, so I skipped the FamilySearch hints review and the profile read.

**Plan pl_001, in order:**
1. pli_001: 1880 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It checks whether Michael was already in the county or mining before 1882.
2. pli_002: 1870 census household and later years (1880 to 1900), FamilySearch. It looks at his earlier household and neighbors and whether he stayed in mining. The 1900 census needs a separate collection lookup.
3. pli_003: City and county directories, 1875 to 1900, FamilySearch. They bracket his arrival and any change of job.
4. pli_004: Deeds, Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, 1870 to 1900, FamilySearch. This is a search on his brother's circle (a FAN item): Patrick, James Kelly and Michael. It tests whether Patrick drew him there. Laborers often leased land rather than bought it, so it includes browsing the deed images.
5. pli_005: Catholic church records, 1870 to 1900, FamilySearch. They may show kin, sponsors or a shared origin. The name-searchable collections come first, then browse-only films (personCount 0).
6. pli_006: Newspapers, 1880 to 1884, other repositories. They give context on mine hiring and may name Michael or his brother.
7. pli_007: Naturalization, 1870 to 1910, FamilySearch. It would give his birthplace and where he lived before. There is a browse-only fallback for the coal-region films.
8. pli_008: Michael's own death or burial entry, 1882 to 1930, FamilySearch. State death registration only began in 1906, so earlier deaths are in church, cemetery or probate records.

The wiki pre-work did not apply because his birth country is unknown. No parentage item was needed, since the question is about motive for the move. The only validation warning was about the jurisdiction wording on pli_002. That wording is slightly off, and the item should be searched at Schuylkill and the 1870 county.

**Hand-back:** search-records for the FamilySearch items (1 to 5, 7, 8). search-external-sites for the newspapers (6).

I made a research plan to find out whether Michael Sheahan really moved to Schuylkill County around 1882 to work in the coal mines, as the family story says. We know he was a farmer in 1870 and a miner in Schuylkill County by 1882, but no record yet explains why he moved. The plan starts with the 1880 census and nearby years to pin down when he arrived. It then checks city directories and the land records of his brother Patrick, who was already there in 1875. After that come church records, newspapers about mine hiring, naturalization papers, and Michael's own death or burial record. Each of these could show where he came from or who brought him.

Next, the FamilySearch record searches will run in that order, starting with the 1880 census. The newspaper search will follow separately.

City and county directories (United States City and Business Directories, name-searchable) give year-by-year residence and occupation. Log_002 found the 1882 entry incidentally. Adjacent years bracket the arrival and show the colliery or town and whether his job changed from laborer to miner.

FAN item. S2 records Patrick Sheahan buying land from James Kelly in 1875 (Deed Book 42, p. 118), and F4 puts Patrick in Schuylkill County in 1875. Tree R2 makes Patrick a sibling of Michael, with the same parent entry I3. Patrick may have drawn Michael to the county. Search deeds, mortgages and later conveyances for either brother, and for James Kelly, as grantor, grantee or witness. Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds is name-searchable but covers little. Coal-region laborers often leased rather than bought (loc_001), so also browse the Recorder of Deeds images.

FAN item. Catholic parish registers (Diocese of Philadelphia then, per loc_001) held at the parish or diocese record Michael's and Patrick's marriages, baptisms of their children, and sponsors. These could show kin or a shared origin community that drew them to the coal region. Use Pennsylvania Births and Christenings and County Marriages, which are name-searchable, then browse-only church films (personCount 0 per loc_001) for the Schuylkill parishes.

Local papers (Pottsville and the mining towns) for 1880-1884 may report mine openings, labor demand, strikes, accidents or hiring in the years around 1882, which is context that tests the coal-work motive. They may also name Michael, his brother or an employer. Check Chronicling America and paid newspaper sites for these titles.

The surname suggests Irish origin, but the tree does not state it. A naturalization declaration or petition states birthplace, arrival date, residence, and often occupation, and may show where he lived before Schuylkill. Pennsylvania naturalization collections are name-searchable for several districts, but loc_001 notes some coal-region films are browse-only, so plan an image browse as the fallback.

Michael's own death or burial entry, which also serves as the origin-of-life check. Statewide death registration starts only in 1906 (loc_001), so a death before then lives in church, cemetery or probate records. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and Cemetery Records are name-searchable. They may state age, birthplace and occupation, such as a mining death, and name an informant who is kin. Also check the Schuylkill Haven funeral home obituary cards.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Mode: create. This is the first plan for q_001, "Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?"

What the project already records:
- **Tree F1:** residence in 1870, "Pennsylvania" only.
- **Tree F2 and F3:** residence in Schuylkill County in 1882, occupation Miner.
- **log_001:** the 1870 census shows him as a farmer in a household outside Schuylkill County. The exact county is not in the tree.
- **log_002:** an 1882 directory lists him as a miner in Schuylkill County. Neither record explains the move.
- **Subject profile:** Michael has no FamilySearch ark, so there is no hints item. The question is a hypothesis test, not a parentage question.
- **Wiki pre-work:** I fetched no wiki pages, because none of the triggers applied.

Plan pl_001, in execution order:
1. **pli_001:** 1880 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It shows whether he was in the coal region before 1882, plus his birthplace, occupation and neighbors.
2. **pli_002:** 1870 census, FamilySearch. Re-open the log_001 entry to fix the origin county and household. Later origin-county items depend on it.
3. **pli_003:** City and county directories, Schuylkill, 1878-1890, FamilySearch. Brackets his arrival and shows his residence and occupation.
4. **pli_004:** Newspapers, Pottsville and coal-region papers, 1880-1885, external. These could name a colliery or employer, the likeliest direct mention of the work.
5. **pli_005:** Deeds in the origin county and Schuylkill, 1870-1890, FamilySearch. A farm sale around 1880-82 would show him leaving farming. Coal laborers usually leased land, so a missing Schuylkill purchase proves nothing.
6. **pli_006:** Marriage and baptism records, Schuylkill, 1870-1895, FamilySearch. They give residence, occupation and sponsors (FAN names). Catholic registers may be browse-only.
7. **pli_007:** Naturalization, Schuylkill, 1870-1910, FamilySearch. This applies only if he was foreign-born, so it depends on the 1880 census.
8. **pli_008:** His own death, burial and obituary entries, 1882-1940, FamilySearch. These often say when and why a man came to the region.

No item is a fallback for another. The question is a hypothesis test, so I did not plan a dedicated parents' marriage item. FAN leads (neighbors, sponsors, grantors) are folded into pli_001, pli_005 and pli_006. Two validation warnings came back about place wording on pli_002 and pli_004. Both fall inside the Pennsylvania locality, and the plan was written successfully.

Hand-off: pli_001 to pli_003 and pli_005 to pli_008 go to search-records. pli_004 (newspapers) goes to search-external-sites.

This plan tests whether Michael Sheahan came to the Pennsylvania coal region around 1882 to work in the mines, as the family story says. We already know he was a farmer in 1870 somewhere outside Schuylkill County and a miner there by 1882. Nothing yet says why he moved.

The plan starts with the 1880 and 1870 censuses, which show where he lived, what he did and who lived near him. It then checks directories and local newspapers for a mining employer. After that come land sales, marriage and baptism records, naturalization papers, and his own death notice or obituary, any of which might say why he came.

Next, the census and directory searches will be run first, since they are free, searchable, and fix both ends of the move.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

entry.rationale: The tree already cites a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) for Patrick's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, but no assertion has been extracted from it. Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so a 1908 certificate exists and normally names the father and mother and the informant. Pull the certificate itself via Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials (name-searchable) and record parents, birthplace and informant. Treat as derivative for parentage.

Timeline t_001 has a medium gap 1851-1860 and the 1860 census is not yet searched. The 1850 census (Thomas Flynn household, dwelling 84, Patrick age 5, born Ireland) does not state relationships, so a_004 is only inferred. 1860 is name-searchable; look for Thomas, a wife and Patrick (age ~15) together, with siblings and variant spellings (Flinn, Flin, Flynne).

Covers the later part of Patrick's life through 1900 (death 1908). The 1880 census is name-searchable and states relationship to head and parents' birthplaces, which can show whether Thomas or a mother lived with Patrick. 1870 and 1900 track the household. Mother's name is unknown; parents could have died or moved in this period.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other: Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland) and a wife of unknown name. It would confirm them as a couple and supply the wife's maiden name if this was her first marriage; the date relative to ~1845 corroborates the 1850 co-residence but does not by itself show Patrick is their child. Use name-searchable Pennsylvania County Marriages and Civil Marriages, plus Church Marriages. The marriage may have occurred in Ireland before emigration, so a miss is expected and not negative proof. Watch for a prior marriage of the wife.

Patrick's own marriage record(s). Birth was ~1845 in Ireland (per the 1850 census, not Pennsylvania as the objective states), so a baptism in a Pennsylvania parish may not exist and Irish registers are largely out of reach. Marriage entries may state age, birthplace or parents' names. Allow for more than one marriage.

Patrick's own burial entry, planned because his birth (~1845, Ireland, before emigration) probably has no accessible baptism. Church burial registers (Catholic parishes under the Diocese of Philadelphia per loc_001, held at the parish) and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records may give age or birthplace and place him beside parents or siblings in the same plot. Also search for Thomas Flynn's burial.

Probate or administration for Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818), and for a possible mother. Window is set by the parents' lifespans: Thomas could die anywhere from 1850 to about 1900 or later, not just within Patrick's life. Register of Wills holds records from 1811 (loc_001). Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is name-searchable but very sparse, and Wills and Deeds is also available. A will or an administration naming heirs would be direct evidence. A Patrick estate (1908) could name siblings or his mother.

FAN item: baptisms, marriages and burials of siblings of Patrick, born after the family arrived in Pennsylvania, would name both parents including the mother's maiden name. Use Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings (name-searchable) and Catholic parish registers (held at parish or diocese). Also check godparents and sponsors, and neighbors near dwelling 84 in the 1850 census, who may be kin or townspeople from the same Irish origin.

Naturalization of Thomas and Patrick Flynn (Irish-born) and obituary or newspaper notices for Patrick, 1908. Naturalization papers can give the immigration date and origin. Some anthracite-region naturalization films are browse-only image groups (loc_001), so check volume_search for those. A 1908 obituary or Civil War service (Pennsylvania Register of Military Volunteers 1861-1865, name-searchable, Patrick age ~16-20) may name parents or kin.

- A Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) is cited for Patrick's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County. No parent names have been extracted from it.
- ps_001 is at tier "possible". Only the 1850 census has been searched. The 1860 census gap in timeline t_001 is still open.
- The tree person has no FamilySearch ark, so I planned no hints-review item. The wiki pre-work isn't triggered: he was born in the British Isles, and no compound surname applies.
- His birth was in Ireland before emigration, so a baptism probably doesn't exist. The plan therefore includes his own death/burial entry (pli_009) and marriage entry (pli_008).

**Plan pl_002 (all FamilySearch unless noted)**
- pli_004: 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate, Schuylkill County. Extract the parents named and the informant.
- pli_005: 1860 census, Schuylkill County. Look for Thomas, a wife and Patrick together, with siblings.
- pli_006: 1870-1900 censuses. The 1880 census gives relationship and parents' birthplaces.
- pli_007: the parents' marriage to each other, Pennsylvania, 1840-1870. It would give the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, and it doesn't prove Patrick is their child. A miss isn't negative proof, since they may have married in Ireland.
- pli_008: Patrick's own marriage record(s), Schuylkill County, 1865-1895.
- pli_009: Patrick's own burial and cemetery entry, 1908, plus Thomas's burial.
- pli_010: probate for Thomas, a possible mother, and Patrick's estate, 1850-1910. The window is set by the parents' lifespans. Repository is the county Register of Wills.
- pli_011: FAN item. Siblings' baptisms, marriages and burials naming both parents, plus godparents and neighbors near dwelling 84.
- pli_012: naturalization (some of it browse-only), the 1908 obituary and Civil War service for clues to parents or kin.

None of the items is a fallback for another. The next step is to run these with search-records, since all are FamilySearch searches. The probate item (pli_010) may need the county courthouse.

The sibling records could name both parents and the mother's maiden name.

**Research Plan for q_002 — Parents of Martha J (mother of Jimmie Jewel Neal)**

**Mode:** Create | **Question:** q_002 — "Who are the parents of Martha J (mother of Jimmie Jewel Neal, born approximately 1859 in Georgia)?"

---

**What We Know So Far:**
- Martha J Neal (tree person I2) has no FamilySearch ark; only known fact is birth ~1859 in Georgia
- She appears under married-name variants: **Landham** and **Wood**
- She married James M Neal on 31 Jul 1879 in Hill County, Texas (styled "Mattie Landham" — a widow's styling)
- "M J Wood" married W F Lanham on 7 Jan 1869 in Smith County, Texas — if this is Martha, she would have been ~10, raising questions about her birth year or her identity
- An uncited lead places an "M M Wood" household in the 1860 census in Blount County, Alabama

---

**Plan pl_001 — 10 items, in sequence:**

| # | Item | Record Type | Location/Time | Purpose |
|---|------|------------|---------------|---------|
| pli_001 | Census | 1860 Alabama | Blount County | Investigate the Wood household lead |
| pli_002 | Census | 1880 Texas | Hill County | Her age, parents' birthplaces, and neighboring kin |
| pli_003 | Marriage | 1869 Texas | Smith County | Original image: age, bondsman, witnesses, parental consent — tests if M J Wood is Martha |
| pli_004 | Census | 1870 Texas | Smith County | Lanham couple and nearby Wood households |
| pli_005 | Marriage | 1879 Texas | Hill County | Original image; look for earlier Landham marriage record |
| pli_006 | Marriage | 1880–1920 | Texas | Hamby marriage (~1888) and any later marriages |
| pli_007 | Death/Burial | 1890–1950 | Texas & New Mexico | Martha's death, plus Jimmie's 1938 death in Carlsbad (may name mother's maiden name) |
| pli_008 | Probate | 1853–1935 | Hill County, TX | Keyword search for a Wood estate naming Martha as heir |
| pli_009 | Probate | 1860–1900 | Blount County, AL | Fallback if pli_001 finds a plausible Wood household |
| pli_010 | Marriage | 1840–1860 | Blount County, AL | Candidate parents' marriage to each other |

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Entries normally name both parents and four grandparents. Spanish naming custom: father's surname first, mother's second, so García = father, Romero = mother is a lead only; surnames can be reversed or varied in the register.

Dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate parents (a García and a Romero) to each other: confirms them as a couple, gives the mother's maiden name (Spanish women keep their surname, so a marriage entry is reliable for it), and the date relative to about 1843 corroborates parentage. It does not by itself prove she is their child; that needs the baptism or a record placing her with them. Search Spain Catholic Church Records (name-searchable collections in loc_001) and the Santa María marriage books by full text. Marriage entries also name the spouses' parents.

Her own marriage entry (not yet located; spouse unknown) typically names her parents and her birthplace and age, which corroborates or substitutes for a baptism that may be hard to find given an approximate birth year. Search by her name in the Spain Catholic Church Records collection and the full-text Santa María marriage books; she may have married elsewhere in Málaga province.

Her own death or burial entry (church burial register, and civil death register after 1871), dated to the years after she was last known alive. Spanish death entries state age, spouse and the names of her parents, giving an independent parental statement and a check on the birth year. Hedge because the baptism may sit in a parish other than Santa María or be misindexed.

FAN item: baptisms of possible siblings (children of the same García and Romero couple) and the godparents named in her baptism and theirs, who are often relatives. Sibling entries naming the same parents and grandparents corroborate which García-Romero couple is hers. Window spans the parents' likely childbearing years before and after 1843.

Notarial protocols and wills/estate division of the candidate parents, who could die from the 1840s to about 1900 (window set by the parents' lifespans, not hers). A will or inheritance division naming her as daughter would be direct evidence. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Per the Denmark Military Records page and loc_001, levying rolls (laegdsruller) from 1788/89 list boys from birth under their father's name, so this is direct parentage evidence and tracks the father year by year. Denmark, Military Levying Rolls (Laegdsruller), 1789-1861 is a FamilySearch collection; if place fields only rank results, browse the Thisted Amt rolls for the Stagstrup parish by hand. Search Mikkel Nielsen with variants (Michel, Mikael, Blyeberg, Bleyberg).

Browse register images because of the low name-indexing in loc_001; check adjoining parishes since brides often married in their home parish.

FAN/sibling item: baptisms of siblings naming the same Niels and mother, and godparents at those baptisms, help test which Niels is the father and reveal kin. Danish naming patterns (first son named for the father's father) help interpret the sibling set.

The 1787 and 1801 Danish censuses list households with relationships; Mikkel (about 8 and 22) may appear in his father's household, bridging the baptism and the levy roll. Verify the collection's availability on FamilySearch when searching; browse if not name-searchable.

Subject's own marriage entries (and any later ones): they often state age, home parish and sometimes the father's name, and name witnesses who may be kin. Mikkel was about 20-40 when marrying; also gives his later residence for the burial item.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

Search Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (1417491) once to confirm or rule out the premise; do not accept a same-named match of a different Elijah Wilkins without matching age, birthplace and Muhlenberg residence.

Per loc_001, probate is the primary death evidence before 1911. Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (1875188) is browse-only per the locality entry, so browse Muhlenberg County will books and order books, administrator bonds and estate settlements; these bracket the death within months and localize it to the county. Look for the widow or adult sons as administrators. Window runs past 1890 to catch late settlements.

loc_001: county death registers in Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (1804888) cover 1852-1910 but 1860s-1870s coverage is partial and many counties lack surviving registers. Search under Wilkins, Wilkens, Wilkerson variants; a hit gives date, place, age and parents. Cheap to try alongside probate.

Tree records Muhlenberg residence in 1870. Verify he appears in 1870 (last known alive), then check 1880 (and 1900 mortality-era households) for him or a widow Wilkins; the first census without him brackets death. 1880 gives relationship to head, helping confirm identity. 1890 schedules largely lost, so rely on 1880 and 1900. Also check the 1870 and 1880 mortality schedules for a death in the preceding year.

Church burial registers, cemetery transcriptions and Find a Grave in Muhlenberg County (loc_001 quirks) can give a stone date and burial place when no register or certificate survives; Kentucky, Deaths and Burials (1804888) also carries burial entries. Gravestone age corroborates birth c. 1814 for identity.

FAN and estate-linked records: tax lists show the last year he is assessed, and deeds by heirs conveying his land (heirs of Elijah Wilkins, deceased) date the death and name sons or a widow, which also confirms identity against other Elijah Wilkinses. Window extends to 1900 because heirs often sell years after death.

items.guide_markdown:
## Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico - 1880-1920

Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Birth about 1895 in Guadalajara for I1, no parents. Baptism entry names parents directly. Mexico, Jalisco, Catholic Church Records, 1590-2022 is name-searchable (loc_001); the Mexico, Baptisms, 1560-1950 collection is also name-searchable. Per loc_001 quirks, search the paternal surname Hernández alone with a wide year window (birth is only approximate), then Ramírez, then through parents without the child's name. Baptism may name godparents, which are FAN leads.

Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 is name-searchable (loc_001); civil registration was in force in 1895, so a birth act may name both parents and grandparents. Search Hernández with variants (Hernandes, Fernández) and the Guadalupe/María name combinations, since the first name used may be Guadalupe rather than María (Mexico Naming Customs).

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, via civil registration (name-searchable) and Jalisco Catholic church marriages; Mexico, Marriages, 1570-1950 is effectively browse-only (personCount 4654 is tiny against its record count), so use the Jalisco collections first. It confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's name, and its date relative to about 1895 corroborates a candidate pair. It does not alone prove María Guadalupe is their child. Women keep their own surname in Mexican records, but a remarriage is possible, so the surname Ramírez is treated as unverified until a record names her parents.

The subject's own marriage (civil and Catholic) is a primary route if the baptism is not found or the birth year is off: marriage acts typically state age, birthplace and parents' names. Plan a search of the Jalisco civil registration and church collections, as Guadalajara residence at marriage is unproven.

The subject's own death or burial entry, dated across her whole adult life since her death date is unknown; death acts usually name parents and age. Search Jalisco civil registration (to 2000) and Mexico, Deaths, 1680-1940 (name-searchable) under Hernández and under any married surname found in item 4. The baptism could be missing or unindexed, so end-of-life records give an independent route to parents.

FAN item: siblings' baptisms and civil births. Search parents-only (a parent's first surname, omitting the child's name) as loc_001 recommends, for children of a Hernández and Ramírez couple. Siblings' records place children with the parents and supply parent names and godparents, testing which couple has María Guadalupe in the household. The window spans the likely childbearing years of parents of a child born about 1895.

FAN item: baptisms, marriages and deaths of the subject's own children, which can name her as mother and sometimes her parents as grandparents or godparents. Dependent on finding her spouse via item 4. A later, indirect source used to corroborate, not to establish, parentage.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
